You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",

      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {

     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",

     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {

     ],

    },
    {

     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Requirements:
        *   $V_{out, min} \ge 4.5\text{ V}$
        *   $V_{out, max} \le 5.5\text{ V}$
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$
        *   $T_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$
        *   $\Delta V \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (settled)
    *   Piezo Source: Sinusoidal current $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $20\text{ M}\Omega$ resistance.
    *   Reference: FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) fails $V_{out, min}$, $V_{out, max}$ (on S3), and $T_{up}$.

    *   The previous attempts used SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) topologies.
    *   `p_sshi_full_bridge` and `p_sshi_half_bridge` both achieved $V_{out, min}$ easily (even over-voltage), meaning the energy harvesting is efficient.
    *   *Critical Failures*:
        *   $V_{out, max}$ is violated: The output voltage goes way above $5.5\text{ V}$ because there's no regulation.
        *   $\Delta V$ and $V_{pp}$ are violated: The output is drifting and ripple is high. This suggests the storage capacitor $C_1$ is either too small (ripple) or the charging current is too high/pulsed relative to the load (drift). Wait, the drift $\Delta V$ refers to the mean difference between two windows. If $V_{out}$ is still rising, it hasn't settled. If it's too high, it's because the harvested power >> load power.

    *   The current harvested power is much higher than needed (screening shows $700-2800\%$ of required power).
    *   We need a way to clamp the output voltage to the $4.5\text{ V} - 5.5\text{ V}$ range.
    *   A Zener diode (`DZ33`) is available, but it clamps at $3.3\text{ V}$, which is too low (we need $4.5\text{ V}-5.5\text{ V}$).
    *   Wait, the goal is $4.5\text{ V}$ to $5.5\text{ V}$. The `DZ33` is a $3.3\text{ V}$ Zener. If I put it in series with a diode, I get $3.3 + 0.25 \approx 3.55\text{ V}$. Still too low.
    *   Alternatively, I can use a shunt regulator or a simpler approach: if the SSHI is too efficient, maybe a simpler rectifier or a different SSHI configuration? But the SSHI is good for low-voltage sources.
    *   Let's look at the $V_{out, max}$ failure. The output voltage is climbing because the energy is being pumped into $C_1$ and there is no mechanism to stop it once it reaches $5.5\text{ V}$.
    *   Since we have no active voltage regulator (like a LDO or a buck converter), we must rely on the inherent properties of the circuit or a passive clamp.
    *   Is there a way to use the Zener `DZ33`? A Zener clamp on `out` to `0` will clamp at $3.3\text{ V}$. That fails $V_{out, min} \ge 4.5\text{ V}$.
    *   Wait, I can't use the Zener to clamp at $5\text{ V}$ directly.

    *   Maybe the SSHI is "too" good. Let's try a different topology.
    *   A standard SSHI uses a switch and an inductor to flip the voltage on $C_p$.
    *   If the output is too high, maybe we can use a slightly less efficient rectifier or increase the load? No, the load is fixed.
    *   We need a way to bleed off excess energy. A resistor in parallel with $C_1$? That would just waste power and might make S4 (weak excitation) fail.
    *   Wait, look at the $V_{out, max}$ failure again. The voltage is climbing. This is a classic problem in energy harvesting: the open-circuit voltage of the harvester is higher than the target.
    *   If we use a Full Bridge Rectifier (FBR), the $V_{out}$ was $2.2\text{ V}$ to $7\text{ V}$. For S3 (strong excitation), it reached $7.13\text{ V}$ (FAIL).
    *   The SSHI is effectively a DC-DC converter. By adjusting the timing and components, we can influence the output voltage. But usually, the output voltage settles where $P_{harvested} = P_{load}$. If $P_{harvested} \gg P_{load}$, $V_{out}$ will keep rising until it hits the piezo's open-circuit voltage limit (or the components break).

    *   If we can't use a regulator, maybe we can use a "leaky" path that only conducts at high voltages?
    *   The `DZ33` Zener breaks down at $3.3\text{ V}$. If I put a diode `DSCH` in series with the Zener (`0` -> `DSCH` -> `DZ33` -> `out`), the total clamp voltage would be $V_{forward} + V_{zener} \approx 0.25 + 3.3 = 3.55\text{ V}$. Still too low.
    *   What if I put two Zeners in series? `0` -> `DZ33` -> `DZ33` -> `out`. $3.3 + 3.3 = 6.6\text{ V}$. Too high ($V_{out, max} \le 5.5\text{ V}$).
    *   What if I use a silicon diode `DSI` (0.5 V) and a Zener? $0.5 + 3.3 = 3.8\text{ V}$. Still too low.
    *   Wait, what if I use the Zener as part of a different structure? Or what if I just use a very large $C_1$ to slow down the rise? No, that hurts $T_{up}$ and "settled".

    *   Wait! The goal is $4.5\text{ V}$ to $5.5\text{ V}$.
    *   Maybe the problem is that $C_1$ is too small, causing high ripple and the mean to drift? $2.2\text{ \mu F}$ might be too small for a $100\text{ Hz}$ source with high-energy pulses from SSHI.
    *   Try $C_1 = 10\text{ \mu F}$ or $22\text{ \mu F}$.
    *   But the most pressing issue is $V_{out, max}$.

    *   The output of an SSHI typically settles at a voltage related to the peak voltage of the piezo.
    *   $V_{out} \approx V_{pzp, peak} \times (\text{efficiency factor})$.
    *   If we use a half-bridge SSHI, we only harvest from one half-cycle. This reduces the power.
    *   Let's look at the results of `p_sshi_half_bridge` (Design 2):
        *   S4: $V_{avg} = 4.95\text{ V}$, $V_{max} = 5.31\text{ V}$. (PASSES $V_{out, min}$ and $V_{out, max}$!)
        *   S1: $V_{avg} = 9.28\text{ V}$, $V_{max} = 9.6\text{ V}$. (FAIL $V_{out, max}$)
        *   S2: $V_{avg} = 9.14\text{ V}$, $V_{max} = 9.49\text{ V}$. (FAIL $V_{out, max}$)
    *   So, the half-bridge SSHI is closer. We just need to lower the output for the stronger conditions.

    *   Is there a way to limit the energy transfer?
    *   We could add a series resistor between the rectifier and the storage capacitor. This would create a voltage drop $I_{rect} \times R_{series}$.
    *   $I_{rect}$ is pulsed. This might increase ripple.
    *   Alternatively, use a larger capacitor $C_1$ to reduce ripple and a slightly different SSHI timing to lower the voltage.
    *   Actually, the "settled" and "ripple" failures are likely because $C_1$ is too small. $2.2\text{ \mu F}$ is quite small for a $100\text{ Hz}$ system. Let's try $47\text{ \mu F}$ (max is $47\text{ \mu F}$).
